subject: Vocabulary
description: Hypothesis, theory, observation, peer review, replication, paradigm — exam-frequent

questions.stem: In science, a HYPOTHESIS is best understood as:

options.option_text: A confirmed law that has never been challenged
A testable, tentative explanation for an observation
A mathematical proof obtained from existing axioms
A philosophical opinion that cannot ever be verified

questions.explanation: HYPOTHESIS — Greek 'hypo' (under) + 'thesis' (placing); 'an under-laid claim'. Tentative, testable explanation; can be supported or refuted by experiment / observation. THEORY — well-substantiated explanation supported by extensive evidence (e.g., theory of evolution, theory of relativity). LAW — concise statement of an observed regularity (e.g., Newton's law of gravity). Distractor 1 — confused with law. Distractor 3 — that's mathematics. Distractor 4 — that's metaphysics.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: PEER REVIEW in academic publishing means that a paper:

options.option_text: Is read aloud at a conference of the author's peers
Is evaluated by anonymous experts in the same field
Is subject to public voting before final acceptance
Is checked by an editor of a competing journal

questions.explanation: Peer review — the journal editor sends the manuscript to 2-3 anonymous experts (peers) in the same subfield. They evaluate methodology, novelty, soundness, and recommend accept / revise / reject. Author often doesn't know identities of reviewers (single-blind) or vice versa (double-blind). Quality-control mechanism in modern science. Distractor 1 confuses peer review with conference talks. Distractor 3 — public voting is not standard. Distractor 4 — competing-journal editor doesn't routinely check.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: An EMPIRICAL claim is one that:

options.option_text: Cannot be tested by any kind of observation
Is based on direct observation or experimental evidence
Is purely deductive, derived from logical axioms only
Is endorsed by the king or government in question

questions.explanation: EMPIRICAL — Greek 'empeiria' (experience). Based on observation, sense-experience, or experiment. Contrasts with: A PRIORI / RATIONAL — derived from reason / logic alone (Distractor 3). Distractor 1 = un-falsifiable claim (a problem in science). Distractor 4 = appeal to authority (a logical fallacy). Empirical claims are the bedrock of natural science; falsifiability (Karl Popper) — a true scientific claim must in principle be testable + refutable.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A PARADIGM SHIFT (Thomas Kuhn) refers to:

options.option_text: A small refinement to existing scientific knowledge
A fundamental change in basic concepts and practices
Replacement of one government's leader with another
A change of textbook used in a single university

questions.explanation: Thomas Kuhn — 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962). Normal science proceeds within a 'paradigm' (set of shared assumptions). When anomalies accumulate, a 'paradigm shift' occurs — a fundamental rethink. Examples: Ptolemy → Copernicus (geo to helio); Newton → Einstein (absolute to relative); classical → quantum mechanics; geology's continental drift; oncology's gene-targeted therapy. The phrase has become widely used outside science (often loosely). Distractor 1 = 'normal science' (refinement). Distractor 3, 4 = misuses of the term.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: REPLICATION in scientific research is important because:

options.option_text: Repeating a study wastes time and money to no avail
It tests whether the original result is reliable and reproducible
It allows authors to publish the same paper multiple times
It proves that scientific theories never need to be revised

questions.explanation: Replication — independent re-running of an experiment to confirm the original result. Failures of replication, especially in psychology + social sciences (the 'replication crisis' since ~2010s), have prompted reforms: pre-registration of hypotheses, open data, larger sample sizes, paying more attention to effect sizes. A single experiment is rarely conclusive; reliable knowledge requires REPLICATION across labs and decades. Distractor 1 — replication is essential, not wasteful. Distractor 3 = self-plagiarism, unethical. Distractor 4 — replication, when failing, prompts theory revision.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: CORRELATION vs CAUSATION — a common scientific reminder is that:

options.option_text: Two correlated events always cause one another
Correlation does not imply causation by itself
Causation always requires a strong correlation first
Correlation is irrelevant to scientific reasoning at all

questions.explanation: Correlation = two variables move together statistically. Causation = one variable directly influences the other. Correlation may arise from: (a) genuine causation A→B; (b) reverse causation B→A; (c) common cause / confounder; (d) coincidence; (e) selection bias. The classic example: ice-cream sales correlate with drowning rates → both caused by hot weather (confounder), not by each other. Establishing causation needs randomised controlled trials, instrumental variables, or natural experiments. Distractor 1 — too strong; correlation doesn't always imply causation. Distractor 3 — backwards (causation IMPLIES correlation, not the reverse). Distractor 4 — overstates the criticism.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A PLACEBO-CONTROLLED trial is one in which:

options.option_text: All participants receive only the active drug studied
Some participants receive an inactive substance for comparison
All participants receive a different existing drug regimen
Only the lead investigator knows which group is which

questions.explanation: Placebo-controlled trial: one group gets the test drug, the other gets a PLACEBO (sugar pill / inert). Differences in outcome attributable to the drug, not to expectation or natural recovery. Often DOUBLE-BLIND (neither participant nor researcher knows assignment) to avoid bias. The gold standard in clinical research. Distractor 1 — without control, can't separate drug effect. Distractor 3 = active-control trial (different design — e.g., compares new drug to current standard). Distractor 4 = single-blind, weaker than double-blind.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The term OSMOSIS specifically refers to the movement of:

options.option_text: Solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution
Solute particles across a membrane towards zones of lower concentration gradient
Any substance through a membrane regardless of concentration or applied pressure
Water molecules from a concentrated to a dilute solution via active transport mechanism

questions.explanation: Osmosis is the passage of solvent (usually water) through a semipermeable membrane from a region of low solute concentration (dilute, high water potential) to high solute concentration (concentrated, low water potential). Option D is doubly wrong: it reverses the direction and incorrectly labels the process as active transport, which requires cellular energy and moves substances against gradients.

questions.stem: A CATALYST accelerates a chemical reaction primarily by:

options.option_text: Being permanently consumed and incorporated into the final reaction product
Increasing the reaction temperature to supply energy to the reactant molecules
Lowering the activation energy needed for the reaction to proceed efficiently
Supplying additional heat energy directly to reactants to overcome energy barriers

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, enabling more reactant molecules to clear the energy barrier per unit time. Crucially, a catalyst is not consumed — it is recovered unchanged at the end. Option A (consumed in reaction) defines a reactant, not a catalyst. Options B and D confuse raising temperature (kinetic effect) with reducing activation energy (mechanistic effect).

questions.stem: The HALF-LIFE of a radioactive isotope is correctly defined as the time taken for:

options.option_text: The isotope to lose exactly half its total mass through radioactive decay processes
The radiation emitted by a sample to drop to half its initially measured intensity
The energy output of the isotope to reduce to exactly 50% of the initial release rate
Half the nuclei in a given sample to undergo spontaneous radioactive disintegration

questions.explanation: Half-life (t½) is defined in terms of the number of radioactive nuclei: the time for exactly half the atoms in a sample to decay into daughter nuclei. Option A is wrong because mass loss is not the defining criterion — daughter nuclei remain in the sample. Option B confuses activity (disintegrations per second) with the count of undecayed nuclei, though activity does halve over one half-life for different reasons.

questions.stem: HOMEOSTASIS in living organisms specifically refers to the ability to:

options.option_text: Adapt permanently to external environments across successive generations of offspring
Regulate reproductive cycles in response to seasonal and photoperiod environmental cues
Store nutrients and energy reserves within tissues for use during adverse conditions
Maintain a stable internal environment despite fluctuations in external conditions

questions.explanation: Homeostasis (from Greek homoios = similar, stasis = standing) is the physiological process of keeping internal variables — body temperature, blood pH, glucose levels — within narrow limits irrespective of external changes, via negative-feedback mechanisms. Option A describes evolutionary adaptation over generations, not moment-to-moment regulation. Option B describes photoperiodism, a separate neuroendocrine response.

questions.stem: In thermodynamics, ENTROPY is best understood as a measure of:

options.option_text: The degree of molecular disorder or randomness within a thermodynamic system
The total heat content or enthalpy available within a chemical reaction system
The rate at which thermal energy transfers between two objects in physical contact
The maximum useful work extractable from a system at constant temperature and pressure

questions.explanation: Entropy (S) quantifies the number of microstates available to a system — effectively its disorder or randomness. The Second Law states that entropy of an isolated system spontaneously increases. Option B describes enthalpy (H), not entropy. Option D describes Gibbs free energy (G = H − TS), a concept that combines both enthalpy and entropy but is itself a separate thermodynamic quantity.

questions.stem: The biological process called APOPTOSIS is most precisely characterised as:

options.option_text: Cell death triggered by external trauma, pathogen invasion, or toxic chemical exposure
Uncontrolled rapid multiplication of cells that have evaded programmed death signals
Genetically programmed elimination of damaged or surplus cells without triggering inflammation
Rupture of the cell membrane releasing cytoplasmic contents and activating immune response

questions.explanation: Apoptosis ('programmed cell death') is an orderly, caspase-mediated process directed by the cell's own genome to remove damaged, infected, or developmentally redundant cells. Crucially, it does not spill cell contents, so no inflammation occurs. Option A and D describe necrosis — traumatic, uncontrolled death that does rupture membranes and elicit inflammation. Option B is the opposite: cancer arises precisely when apoptosis fails and cells proliferate unchecked.

questions.stem: QUORUM SENSING in microbiology refers to the mechanism by which bacteria:

options.option_text: Detect and neutralise antibiotic molecules present in the surrounding tissue environment
Transfer genetic material between bacterial cells through plasmid conjugation channels
Form biofilms exclusively by adhering to nutrient-rich inorganic surface substrates
Coordinate collective behaviours by sensing population density through chemical signals

questions.explanation: Quorum sensing is a population-density-dependent signalling system: bacteria continuously secrete small autoinducer molecules and monitor their extracellular concentration. Once the threshold (quorum) is crossed, gene expression switches to coordinate group behaviours — virulence factor production, sporulation, biofilm formation. Option B describes bacterial conjugation (horizontal gene transfer). Option A describes antibiotic-resistance sensing, a separate regulatory pathway not classified as quorum sensing.
